newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn government under siege on jobless crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bonn government under siege on jobless crisis.

text.p: The Bonn government came under fire from all sides on Sunday when trade union officials and business leaders said it was doing little to tackle the weak economy at the heart of the country's jobless crisis.

A new poll, meanwhile, indicated that Germans in the street were, one year ahead of general elections, losing patience with Bonn's record on unemployment, with a clear majority believing that the present government was not up to the task.

Even a flagship tax reform, designed as a 30 billion-mark ($18 billion) "gift" to Germans currently struggling with pre-EMU austerity measures, received the thumbs-down from big business, with most companies saying in a survey it would not spur them into making any new investment.

The growing disillusionment with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government follows January unemployment figures showing an unexpected jump of more than half a million to 4.66 million, the highest level seen in the country since the depression of the early 1930s.

Klaus Zwickel, chairman of Germany's largest trade union, the mighty IG Metall, attacked Kohl for using the cost-cutting required for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) as a reason not to boost public spending in the economy.

"We need more investment impulses, in everything from transport, the environment...through to public services. Of course that costs money -- but the money is there," Zwickel said in an interview with the Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

Proof of that, he said, was the fact that the government could contemplate a tax reform aimed at cutting taxes by 30 billion marks, "most of which will go to the rich, and they won't create more jobs just to please Helmut Kohl."

The most pressing of Kohl's problems is the need to bring public deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product by the end of the year to qualify for entry into the single Eurpoean currency in 1999.

But the higher-than-expected jobless levels have led many economists to assume that Germany will not now be able to bring its deficits down in time, forcing Bonn into the politically embarrassing situation of having to plead for a flexible interpretation of the EMU criteria.
Worse, more public expenditure is now required to kickstart the German economy out of the sluggish growth rates that have led to the costly unemployment problem, some economic forecasters insist.
"We must boost next year's planned public spending levels by at least a further 20 billion marks," Lutz Hoffmann, head of the DIW economic institute, said in a Sunday newspaper interview.

He added that the already huge subsidies flowing into the former Communist-controlled east of the country must at least remain at current levels if east Germany was not to plunge into outright recession.

Any increase in private investment expected as a result of a lowering of corporate taxes as part of the tax reform will, according to a survey of Germany's largest companies published at the weekend, simply not materialise.

Business daily newspaper Boersen-Zeitung said that while a majority of Germany's top businesses welcomed the lower corporate taxes, additional measures in the reform could actually make investment more expensive.

Tax experts at industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG were quoted as saying that harsher rules on how they will be allowed to write off investments, together with planned taxes on currently tax-free night- and Sunday-work, would more than offset the expected gains.
Engineering group Siemens AG estimated that the cost of domestic investment could rise by as much as 10 percent as a result of the reform.

There was also little cheer to be had by the government in a poll conducted on behalf of the N-TV commercial television channel, in which 69 percent of those interviewed believed that the government's employment policies were incorrect.
And while three-quarters thought that unemployment could be reduced with proper job creation measures, a similar number thought that the situation would only get worse in the coming months.
